title: Armstrong is no Uncle Tom: the $500 rebuke
summary: Contradicting the Uncle Tom view of Armstrong and Stepin Fetchit, Butler tells how Armstrong rebuked an impresario rubbing his head for luck by demanding $500.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well, you know, that's a very interesting thing, since we're on the subject, because a lot of people tend to think that many of the guys like Stepen Fetchit, Louis Armstrong, who came out of that area, were Uncle Tom's. They were strategists.
Oh, no. No, man, no. / Louis Armstrong (inaudible) I'll give you an instance, I thought Louis Armstrong was tomming something terrible, I thought.
We were in a little cabaret one time, we were talking, everybody was having fun --
By the way, what year is this?

This is around '63 or '64. Louis Armstrong invited me there. And there was a -- he was an impresario. And he was so rubbing Louis Armstrong's head, just drumming it. And Louis ignored it. And I started to tell him, Louis, what is that man doing on your head? Louis Armstrong didn't say nothing. But then, about a half hour later he says, now, you have had your pleasure. You feel that you're going to have luck. Now, I'm going to get my luck now. You owe me $500.00 and I'm going to take it out of your share of what you're supposed to have.

He said, "Yeah, but I was -- you don't quite understand what you was doing. You were satisfying yourself on my head thinking you would have luck on this nigger's head. Now, this nigger want $500.00, right now. And he went, "Oh, I'm so sorry." "Don't be sorry. You can't do that ever again." If it had been you or I would have been in a big fight but that man was hurt more, because it was in front of everybody. Everybody was looking, everybody being uncomfortable. (Inaudible). And Louis just kept quiet. (Inaudible).
